description:
Sponsor: Thermalright Frozen Prism 360 on Amazon - https://geni.us/FUqbQC
This review of the NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5060 benchmarks the GPU vs. alternatives like the RTX 4060, RTX 3060, RTX 2060, and even GTX 1060 6GB. The tests of the RTX 5060 Ti (16GB) and RTX 4060 Ti (16GB) also show that the 5060 is overall surrounded by cards with more VRAM, including older cards like the RX 6700 XT. The next benchmarks will look at the AMD RX 9060 XT, so we're keeping this one a bit lighter today as the 9060 XT review will post in short order. We'd encourage checking back for that. For now, this looks at the RTX 5060's performance despite NVIDIA's best efforts to bury it during a Computex launch.

comments.text:
After a week of use, here’s my honest review of the Asus Dual OC RTX 5060, which I got for €272 on sale from Amazon. It also came with a free Asus TUF M3 Gen II mouse, a nice extra to have as a backup.

🔧 I upgraded from an RX 6650 XT, and the difference is huge. The RTX 5060 delivers a much smoother experience, especially when it comes to 1% lows, which are rock solid now. With the 6650 XT, I was getting frequent drops. Cooling is also excellent: 30 °C idle with the fans off, and no more than 40-45 °C under load, even in demanding games.

📈 Game performance:

Valorant (low settings)

RX 6650 XT: ~240 FPS, not stable

RTX 5060: 500+ stable FPS


Fortnite (performance mode)

RX 6650 XT: 240–300 FPS with drops down to 110

RTX 5060: 400–600 FPS stable



In AAA titles, the performance gain is around 20–30% in favor of the RTX 5060. And that’s without even using DLSS. With DLSS enabled, the gap becomes even wider.

🖥️ All tests were done using a Ryzen 5 7600. Keep in mind, the RX 6650 XT had Smart Access Memory (SAM) enabled, yet the RTX 5060 still came out on top across the board.

🔚 Bottom line: I don’t regret the upgrade at all. Fantastic performance, great thermals, and rock-solid stability. A top-tier GPU for 1080p competitive gaming and beyond.

comments.text:
The point about VRAM getting a 33% increase over 10 years made me interested in how regular RAM compares.

Long story short, I calculated the RAM amount average from Steam hw survey. Average right now is 23.09 GB, and average in 2016 was reasonably anywhere from 6.45 to 9.63 GB depending on how you interpret the "12 GB or more" entry that's sitting at 15.83% in the survey: 6.45 GB corresponds to "12 GB or more" = 12 GB, 9.63 GB to "12 GB or more" = 32 GB. So the overall RAM increase is anywhere from 139.92% to 257.78%, probably closer to the latter. If you look at the most popular options, which are 16 GB, and 8 GB, respectively, there's been probably an overall doubling.

To me personally, it felt like it'd be higher until I started crunching the numbers, but that's probably because the overall speed and efficiency of all components also increased over time. The memory is faster now than it was in 2016, so are the processors, but most importantly, so is the storage, as even the swap, which contains stuff that the RAM can't fit, is now written to an SSD, which is, on average, way faster than a hard drive from 2016. You almost forget that, while it feels like things aren't going well, they still are technically better than ever before.

RTX 5060 Review – Efficiency Over Everything
The RTX 5060 is a head-scratcher. For a next-gen GPU, it struggles to impress where it counts. Performance gains are minimal over the previous gen, pricing is questionable, and VRAM capacity feels tight for 2025 standards.

But credit where it’s due: the power efficiency is solid. With a 170W TDP, it runs cooler, quieter, and demands less from your PSU—making it a decent choice for compact or low-power builds.

Still, unless you're laser-focused on efficiency, it’s hard to justify the upgrade. The 5060 gets the watts right—but not much else.

I get wanting to compare the hardware, but I feel like a section comparing enhancements would be more representative of real-world usage for most people. I get the statistical reduce the variables aspect, but I do wish we had a section on enhancements and image quality or a separate video, since the software aspects are just inextricably linked to the hardware, and it informs the purchase decision.

Again, I get the logic, I think, I'm just not sure it's a useful way to do it, but this is very much debatable, doing it the other way could easily be criticized as well, which is why I think doing both would be nice.

comments.text:
unpopular opinion. I don't think the 5060 is that bad considering the 3060Ti launched at $400 and the 5060 has the same or 10% better performance for $100 less. Yes, I understand that previous generations uplifts were maybe higher and it has been almost 5 years since the 3060Ti launch. But keeping in mind the inflation we have seen over those past 5 years, I don't think that is a bad GPU. Also, it is a fifth generation of RTX and has better DLLS and fake frames technology. I think that those are good points in this case, since this is a budget GPU and you get the opportunity to squeeze some frames. I am not trying to glaze NVIDIA, don't get me wrong, but I don't think the 5060 is THAT bad.

About the performance per dollar. This is what Claude came up with:

"To calculate the performance-to-price ratio, I'll use FPS per dollar as the metric.
RTX 5060:

Let's assume the RTX 3060 Ti gets 100 FPS as a baseline
RTX 5060 gets 10% more = 110 FPS
Price: $300
Performance-to-price ratio: 110 FPS ÷ $300 = 0.367 FPS per dollar

RTX 3060 Ti:

Baseline performance: 100 FPS
Price: $400
Performance-to-price ratio: 100 FPS ÷ $400 = 0.25 FPS per dollar

Result: The RTX 5060 would offer about 47% better value than the 3060 Ti (0.367 vs 0.25 FPS per dollar)."


So you get 47% better value compared to 5 years ago with more RTX features. I don't think that is a bad deal.


Thanks for reading!

comments.text:
I just need an AMD card to come within 10% of top end nVidia performance, and at 70% of the price. The card can be inefficient as hell, and as large and that’s fine by me.

Also, the occupying only half of the PCIe gen5 x16 lanes is definitely a non-issue. RTX4090 barely saturates PCIe gen3 x16, which is PCIe gen4 x8 speed, and PCIe gen5 x4. The only time the difference faster PCIe lanes would make a difference is when/if you're intentionally overrunning VRAM and letting games use normal RAM as an overflow. But even PCIe x16 is massively too slow for GPU usage and your framerates are already tanked. Maybe you saved your 5060 from 4fps, and got it up to 8fps in those scenarios. A doubling sounds great, but it's only a doubling of performance in areas where your card is already performing extremely bad compared to where it should be in the first place. Everyone is going to sensibly conclude that reducing settings to avoid the VRAM overflow to regain performance is the choice to make in that trade off.

comments.text:
Nvidia doesn't just come with frame generation, but model tier generation now. Your "5050" became a "5060"... 

Sure, the model numbers have always been somewhat arbitrary, but they used to signify "replacement" or "upgrade" over time. Ie. you would upgrade from a 10 series to a 30 series or a 1060 to a 2070. or replace a 2060 with a 3060 or something like that. 

Now I'm wondering that maybe it was a bad choice for AMD to switch naming scheme to match Nvidia, because that trust or knowledge is evaporating fast...

...

I don't think there's any way avoiding general price increases, inflation, that AI pays more and thus gives more incentive, but also that increased performance is harder to get and does come at a cost. 

On the other hand I also think gaming is arriving at some sort of plateau soon, where the graphics become so good, that improvements become of minor importance and other aspects of games such as details in eg. nps (AI?), physical interactivity (physx?) and hopefully good story and universe become predominant factors... 

We aren't there yet... aka. it's not the end of the (gaming) world... but you can see it from here.
